The systematic literature review (SLR) operates as a structured probabilistic inference engine over a corpus of scholarly works. It applies Bayesian-like logic through staged inclusion criteria—title, keyword, abstract, and quality review—to estimate posterior probabilities of relevance. Each stage acts as a conditional update on the likelihood of a paper contributing to the field of computational intelligence in sports. The resulting technique and topic distributions are descriptive statistics derived from this process. However, its limitations stem from the truncation of Semantic Scholar results, lack of reproducible search queries, and reliance on dated inclusion windows. These issues introduce bias and reduce internal validity. The SLR's failure mode lies in its inability to scale beyond static categorization, unlike GSE's dynamic, state-transition-based reasoning engines that evolve with new data and models. In contrast, GSE employs deep learning architectures such as TFT and GNNs, which are not captured in this review’s taxonomy. Thus, while the SLR provides a historical snapshot, it lacks the predictive power and adaptability required for modern sports intelligence systems.
